citation: docs/architecture.md, ownership of truth (the core owns composition; cursors are written, not read) and durability (Muster's own durable state is composition, and only composition)
why: Composition is the only thing Muster owns rather than mirrors, which makes it the only thing it can get wrong on its own. Every other picture in the app converges on a daemon's answer eventually; this one has no authority above it to be corrected by. What it holds is a window's ordered list of Muster tabs, which of them is on screen, and how each is divided between the machines holding panes in it (MIP-2). Three properties carry the file. View-local focus is written and never read back: which pane this window's keyboard feeds is Muster's decision, so another client moving daemon focus must not yank it, and the case that pins that is the one where a reconcile leaves a working focus alone. Composition names daemon things - a tab, a pane - which disappear without asking, and every way they can disappear ends in a window that ignores the keyboard and cannot say why. And a tab left behind keeps its arrangement, which is what makes switching between tabs cost nothing. The cases are written as steps rather than as one call because that is where the bugs are: what a reconcile does to a focus somebody set three steps earlier.

cases.name: a fresh composition is attached to nothing
cases.why: The starting state has to be distinguishable from a window that is set up and showing nothing. No focus at all is the honest answer before a daemon is attached, and the input path reads it as 'this keystroke has nowhere to go' rather than sending it to a pane it invented.

cases.name: a region needs a daemon that is attached
cases.why: A region naming a daemon nobody is connected to renders nothing, forever, and does it silently - there is no pane stream to fail and no error to log. The refusal is returned so the caller says why instead of the window looking broken.

cases.name: the first region takes the keyboard
cases.why: A window with a region in it and no focus ignores the keyboard and cannot say why. The first region opened is the only one it could mean, so it takes focus rather than waiting to be told.

cases.name: a region opened onto a tab picks up its first pane
cases.why: Opening a region says which tab to show; which pane the keyboard feeds is a separate question, and until the daemon has said what is in that tab there is no answer to it. The first reconcile that can see the tab supplies one, so a region opened before the mirror bootstrapped ends up typeable rather than inert.

cases.name: first means first in the tree, not first by id
cases.why: 'The first pane' has to mean the one a user would point at, which is the one the tree puts first. Pane ids are issued in creation order, so a tab whose panes were split in an order other than left-to-right disagrees with them - and id order would put the keyboard in a pane on the far side of the window.

cases.name: a tab whose tree has not arrived still gets a pane
cases.why: herdr publishes a tab's tree on its own event, which may follow the panes it names, so a tab with panes and no tree is an ordinary moment rather than a broken one. A region that waited for the tree would be untypeable for as long as it lasted, and on a quiet tab that is until something else happens. And both panes are on screen while that tree is missing. A region shows a tab and a tab on screen has its panes on screen; the tree says how they are arranged, so a tree that has not arrived yet hides nothing.

cases.name: a tree naming a pane the mirror has not got skips it
cases.why: The tree and the pane list arrive on separate events, so a tree can name a pane the mirror has not been told about yet. Pointing the keyboard at one would give the window a focused pane that nothing can render and nothing can type into, which looks exactly like a hung terminal. The view withholds that tree rather than rendering it without the missing pane: an arrangement that disagrees with the tab's pane list is one no daemon published, and rendering it would tear down the surfaces it omits. On screen is the pane the tab holds, and only that one: a pane the mirror has not been told about is not one the window can be drawing.

cases.name: reconcile leaves a working focus alone
cases.why: Every pane event brings a fresh tree, so reconcile runs constantly. One that re-picked a pane each time would drag the keyboard back to the first pane every time anything in the session moved, which is the same bug as reading daemon focus and just as invisible in a screenshot.

cases.name: a pane whose program exited hands the keyboard back
cases.why: A keyboard pointed at a pane that is gone types into nothing, and says nothing about it - the input path has a pane id and no way to know it is stale. This is the state view-local focus exists to survive, so it resolves here rather than being guarded at every reader.

cases.name: a tab closed from elsewhere closes its region
cases.why: Another client can close the tab this window is showing, and herdr takes its panes with it without announcing them one by one. The region has nothing left to show and no way back, and a window that kept rendering it would be showing a session that does not exist.

cases.name: reconcile answers for one daemon only
cases.why: Streams from different daemons have no mutual order, so what the local daemon just said is no evidence about the devenv's tabs (architecture.md, cross-daemon order is core order). A pass over every region would close a remote region on the strength of a local snapshot - and a dropped VPN would empty the window.

cases.name: detaching a daemon takes its regions and leaves the rest
cases.why: A detached daemon's panes live in a process this window can no longer reach, so its regions have nothing to show. The other daemon's regions are untouched, which is the whole promise of local and remote in one window: losing the tunnel costs the remote half and not the session.

cases.name: closing the focused region moves the keyboard to a survivor
cases.why: Closing a region is a thing the user did, and leaving them with a window that no longer responds to typing is the worst possible answer to it. The first survivor is arbitrary but predictable, and predictable is what a person recovers from.

cases.name: focusing a region that is gone changes nothing
cases.why: A focus intent racing a region that just closed is ordinary - the click was in flight while the daemon said the tab was over - and there is nothing a caller could do about it. Silently keeping the focus that is valid beats clearing it and beats a failure nobody can act on.

cases.name: a region id names one region, ever
cases.why: Ids are what an intent in flight carries. Reusing the number of a closed region would let a keystroke or a divider drag aimed at one region land in whatever took its place, and the two regions may be showing different daemons.

cases.name: attaching a daemon again restates how to reach it
cases.why: Attaching is what happens on every reconnect, and a daemon that came back on a different socket is the same daemon to everyone looking at the window. Adding a second entry would leave two subscriptions to one session and two copies of every pane.

cases.name: a tree that has not caught up does not move the keyboard
cases.why: The pane list and the tree are published separately, so a tab that is mid-split briefly has a tree naming fewer panes than it holds. Reading the tree as evidence that a pane is gone hands the keyboard to another pane and keeps it there, because the tree that arrives a moment later makes the wrong answer valid. It cost an afternoon as a test that passed alone and failed in the suite; the real symptom is a keyboard that jumps to the first pane when you split, sometimes. Both panes the tab still holds are on screen throughout. The tree going backwards is the daemon describing an arrangement, not withdrawing panes, and a window that reported them hidden here would be telling an agent to go and surface what is already in front of somebody.

cases.name: a zoomed tab shows the pane this window's keyboard is on
cases.why: herdr spells zoom as a flag and keeps publishing every pane at its ordinary unzoomed rect, so a renderer handed the tree paints all of them while the daemon is showing one. Resolving it here rather than flagging it for the shell is what keeps the shell renderable-as-told; the flag survives only so the chrome can say so, because a zoomed tab and a one-pane tab look identical. Which pane fills it is this window's own answer and not the daemon's: herdr's flag sits beside its focused pane, and daemon focus is one value shared with every client, so reading it would let another client decide what this window renders. Here that other client zoomed p2 while this window's keyboard is on p1, and p1 is what fills the region - anything else is somebody typing into a pane they cannot see.

cases.name: a font-size chord sizes the pane the keyboard is on and no other
cases.why: Muster sized every pane in the window at once until it did not, on the argument that a grid you read at a glance is harder to read with ragged cell sizes. The grid is fifteen agents doing different jobs, and the one being read closely is worth more room than the one being watched for a colour - so raggedness is the price of being able to say which. This is the case that would still pass under the old behaviour if the view carried one number for the window, and fails the moment a chord reaches a neighbour. The size rides on the pane rather than on a message of its own, because a shell builds a surface from a leaf and joining two messages would draw a pane at the wrong size for as long as they disagreed.

cases.name: putting a pane's text back leaves its neighbour where somebody left it
cases.why: Reset is the only way out of a size somebody has pressed themselves into, and per-pane sizing gives it a second way to be wrong: a reset that reached the window would undo work on panes the person never touched this time. So it is the same one-pane rule as the two directions, and the neighbour keeps what it was given.

cases.name: moving the keyboard inside a zoomed tab moves what is on screen
cases.why: ⌘2 in a zoomed tab used to leave the previous pane filling the region, so the keyboard fed a pane nobody could see. herdr publishes `layout_updated` when a pane appears or goes and never for a focus change (observations/herdr-0.8.0.md section 10), so the cursor its zoom flag sits beside is stale from the moment focus moves - which is why the zoomed pane has to be read off this window's own keyboard rather than off the daemon's. The tab stays zoomed: what moved is which pane fills it, not whether one does.

cases.name: a view spans daemons, in the order the regions sit
cases.why: One window showing a laptop and a devenv side by side is the desideratum this whole layer exists for, and the view is where it becomes one answer rather than two. Order matters because it is the only part of the arrangement Muster owns - a view that sorted its regions would silently rearrange somebody's window.

cases.name: a step moves the keyboard along the tree
cases.why: Reaching every pane from the keyboard is the floor for a window that renders more than one, and the order has to be the one a person sees rather than the one panes were created in. Tree order is that order: left to right, top to bottom, which is how the same panes are laid out on screen.

cases.name: a step past the last pane comes back to the first
cases.why: A window has no edge to bump against, and a step that silently did nothing at the end is indistinguishable from a dead key - which is the failure this whole vocabulary exists to avoid. Wrapping also means the same keystroke reaches every pane without the user tracking where they are in the tree.

cases.name: a step back from the first pane lands on the last
cases.why: The other direction has to wrap the other way, and it is worth its own case because a modulo written once tends to be written for next only - previous then either refuses at the start or walks off the front of the list.

cases.name: a step crosses out of one region into the next
cases.why: Two regions side by side are one window to the person looking at them, so a step that stopped at a region's edge would leave panes no keystroke could reach - and in the arrangement this product is for, those are the panes on the devenv. Stepping is over the window's reading order, not over one region's.

cases.name: stepping a window with nothing in it leaves the keyboard alone
cases.why: A bare `muster` is the renderer check and has no panes at all. A step there must be a refusal the caller can report rather than a focus set to something invented, because a composition naming a pane no daemon holds is the state that renders and ignores the keyboard.

cases.name: a tree that disagrees with the tab's panes is not published
cases.why: A backend publishes a tab's pane list and its arrangement as separate events, and nothing orders them against each other - a tab mid-split briefly has a tree naming fewer panes than it holds, and a subscription that has just bootstrapped replays layout events and walks a tab backwards through arrangements it had minutes ago. Both were measured against herdr 0.8.0. Rendering the stale tree drops every pane it omits, and a dropped pane costs its surface and the bridge feeding it - which then cannot reconnect, so the pane comes back rendering and swallowing every keystroke. Withholding is a state the shell already answers correctly by leaving what it shows alone. All three stay on screen. Withholding the tree leaves the shell drawing what it had, so the answer that says nothing is on screen is the one that would be false.

cases.name: a tree naming a pane the tab does not hold is not published either
cases.why: The other direction, and it arrives the same way: a pane closes, and the tree still naming it is published before or after the pane list drops it. Rendering that tree builds a surface for a pane that is gone, which spawns a bridge that attaches to nothing and a rectangle that will never paint. One rule covers both directions because there is only one question - does this arrangement describe this tab. The two panes the tab still holds are on screen, and the one it does not is in neither answer.

cases.name: a step out of a region with no arrangement lands in one that has it
cases.why: While a region's tree is withheld there is nothing in it to step through, and the keyboard is standing somewhere the window's reading order does not contain. Refusing would make the key look dead for as long as that lasts, which is unpredictable; going to the first pane the window does know about is an answer that is always available and always somewhere the user can see. Every pane in both regions is on screen, the withheld tree included: what is missing there is the order to step through, not the panes themselves.

cases.name: a daemon reached over ssh is a daemon like any other
cases.why: The whole bet of 'local and remote in one window' is that the transport stops at the adapter and nothing above it can tell the difference. This case is where that stops being an aspiration: an ssh endpoint opens a region, reconciles, holds the keyboard and renders the same way a local one does, and the only line anywhere that differs is the one describing how it is reached. If this case ever needs a branch, the bet was wrong. It carries a second thing worth pinning, because both daemons here hold a pane called w1:p1: the step lands on the other pane of the region it was already in, rather than on the identically named pane in the region before it. Position in the order is a (region, pane) pair, and a step that matched on the pane id alone would jump machines.

cases.name: surfacing a tab nothing shows brings it on screen
cases.why: The common shape of attention routing. A pane that finished unseen is almost always in a tab this window is not showing, and going to it means showing that tab - which is a switch rather than a rearrangement, now that a window shows one tab at a time. The tab it was showing keeps its region and its arrangement, so switching back is free.

cases.name: surfacing a tab already on screen changes nothing
cases.why: Following a notification about a pane you are already looking at must be a no-op, not a second region onto the same tab. Two copies of one tab is the multiplexer this project is deliberately not, and it would double every surface in it.

cases.name: surfacing a devenv tab leaves the laptop's tab as it was
cases.why: A window showing a laptop beside a devenv is the arrangement this project exists for, and it survives this change as a tab holding a region on each. Surfacing a devenv tab that is not in it shows that tab instead - it does not take a region out of the one that is, so switching back finds both halves where they were.

cases.name: a tab both machines hold gets a region on each
cases.why: What a tab spanning two machines is made of. Each machine holds its own half - one herdr tab and one pane tree - and each gets a region, side by side in the order they arrived. This is the shape a version 3 arrangement migrates into, and the shape grouping produces.

cases.name: surfacing a third tab leaves the other two holding their arrangements
cases.why: Switching tabs must not cost the tabs you switched away from. Each keeps the regions it had and which of them the keyboard was in, so a window walked through with next-tab comes back to every tab as it was left - which the rule this replaces could not do, because it moved one region between tabs and had nowhere to remember the rest.

cases.name: a tab switched away from keeps the pane its keyboard was on
cases.why: The other half of switching being free. The tab left behind still holds the pane the keyboard was in, so coming back lands there rather than at the start of its tree - and the tab arriving carries its own, which is what the view renders. The rule this replaces had one region for both tabs and had to clear the pane on every switch.

cases.name: a region opens at the same weight as every other
cases.why: Equal shares are the arrangement nobody has to be told about, and they should fall out of the model rather than be a case somebody wrote. Every region starting at one means a window that has never been dragged divides itself evenly for free.

cases.name: moving a boundary gives one side the share it asked for
cases.why: The whole feature: a laptop and a devenv split a window however the user wants rather than evenly forever. A ratio of the pair rather than of the window, because that is what a drag means - and the weights come out in that proportion.

cases.name: a boundary keeps the pair's own width, so nothing else moves
cases.why: What makes a drag local. The two weights still sum to what they summed to before, so every other region in the tab keeps exactly the width it had - which is what the person dragging expects and what a rule dividing the whole tab would break. Three machines rather than two, because a pair is the whole tab when there are only two of them and nothing is left to leave alone.

cases.name: a region cannot be dragged away to nothing
cases.why: The one place a share is clamped. A pane's ratio goes to the daemon untouched because the daemon sizes its own rectangles and refuses what it cannot do; nothing sits behind this one. A region dragged to zero width leaves no divider to grab and no way back - a state a user can reach and not leave.

cases.name: the clamp holds at the other end too
cases.why: The same trap mirrored. Dragging a divider all the way right would strand the region on its right rather than the one on its left, and a rule that only guarded one direction would be half a guard.

cases.name: the last region has no boundary to move
cases.why: There is nothing to its right to divide against. Doing nothing rather than refusing, for the same reason focusing a closed region does nothing: a drag that arrives as the region beside it closes is ordinary, and there is nothing a caller could do about it.

cases.name: a boundary named for a region that is gone moves nothing
cases.why: A drag is a stream of requests and a region can close underneath one. Moving some other line because the ids shifted along would be worse than doing nothing, which is the argument for naming a boundary by a region rather than by an index.

cases.name: right goes to the pane on the right
cases.why: In a plain grid every rule agrees, which is the point of having this case: it is the one a reader checks their understanding against before reading the ones where the rules come apart.

view: r0 tab=w1:t1 columns(rows(w1:p1, w1:p3@0.5), rows(w1:p2, w1:p4@0.5)@0.5)

cases.name: left comes back
cases.why: Reversible, so a user who overshoots can undo it with the opposite key rather than having to work out where they are.

view: r0 tab=w1:t1 columns(rows(w1:p1, w1:p3@0.5), rows(w1:p2, w1:p4@0.5)@0.5)

cases.name: down goes to the pane below
cases.why: The vertical half, which a rule written only for columns would silently fail - and failing silently is what a dead key looks like.

view: r0 tab=w1:t1 columns(rows(w1:p1, w1:p3@0.5), rows(w1:p2, w1:p4@0.5)@0.5)

cases.name: up comes back
cases.why: Same argument as left, one axis over.

view: r0 tab=w1:t1 columns(rows(w1:p1, w1:p3@0.5), rows(w1:p2, w1:p4@0.5)@0.5)

cases.name: a direction with nothing in it moves nothing
cases.why: No wrapping. Falling off the left of the window and reappearing on the right is disorienting in a way stepping through an order is not - and next and previous already wrap, so this one can afford to be predictable. The keyboard stays where it was.

view: r0 tab=w1:t1 columns(rows(w1:p1, w1:p3@0.5), rows(w1:p2, w1:p4@0.5)@0.5)

cases.name: the neighbour is the one actually beside you, not the first in the tree
cases.why: The case the geometric rule exists for. The left column is split near its top and the right near its bottom, so the pane to the left of the bottom-right one is the tall lower-left pane - which is the second child of that subtree. A walk up to the matching-axis ancestor and back down the near side has no way to know that and takes the first child, landing on a thin strip at the top of the screen that the user was not pointing at.

view: r0 tab=w1:t1 columns(rows(w1:p1, w1:p4@0.2), rows(w1:p2, w1:p3@0.8)@0.5)

cases.name: overlap decides between two panes the same distance away
cases.why: Both panes on the right start at the same line, so distance cannot separate them. The one sharing more edge with where the keyboard was is the one straight ahead, which is what a person means by right.

view: r0 tab=w1:t1 columns(rows(w1:p1, w1:p4@0.2), rows(w1:p2, w1:p3@0.8)@0.5)

cases.name: a window holds tabs from two machines and shows one of them
cases.why: The shape this whole model is for. A laptop tab and a devenv tab sit in one list that cmd+1 and cmd+2 walk, and exactly one of them fills the window - which is what every other terminal and every browser has trained the reader to expect, and what the column-per-machine window could not express.

cases.name: showing another tab puts the first one away
cases.why: One tab on screen at a time is the rule, so the panes of the tab that was showing stop being on screen - which is what tells the agent list that a pane nobody is watching has gone quiet, and what stops a bridge being spawned for a pane nothing is drawing.

cases.name: a window somebody asked for does not open onto a tab another window has
cases.why: herdr allows one client per terminal, so a second window opening onto the first one's tab renders panes that refuse to attach and cannot be closed (kan a_2IZ5TL6DQ). What the machine already held is claimed, and the window shows nothing until a tab of its own arrives - which is what the empty window on screen is for.

cases.name: a claimed machine's next tab is the one the window opens onto
cases.why: The other half of the claim: what a fresh window asked for is the tab that appears after it, and nothing has to correlate the answer with the request for that to work. Every tab in the claim stays listed and stays reachable - taking a terminal from another window is a thing somebody may mean, and only Muster doing it uninvited is the bug.

cases.name: a tab the daemon no longer holds leaves the window
cases.why: A tab closed from another client has nothing left to show, and a window still listing it is a caption that goes nowhere. The window moves to whatever took its place rather than to the first tab, which is what every tab strip does when you close the one you are on.

cases.name: a tab spanning two machines opens on the half it can still reach
cases.why: The degradation this model has to pay for (MIP-2, durability). A tab whose devenv is unreachable has to show the panes it can and say nothing about the rest, rather than refusing to open - which is the rule the mirror already follows for a stale daemon, applied to a tab.
